dossier.public_summary: The 557 ppm dip varies from sector to sector and even transit to transit, so it cannot be one stable planet. There is a deep second eclipse about half an orbit away that is about 60% as deep as the first, and the star shows large brightness swings at the same period. Together this looks like an eclipsing stellar companion, not a planet.

reasons.why: Depth changes far beyond errors: 872 ppm in sector 59 vs 355 ppm in sector 73 vs 253 ppm in sector 86 (depth_change_pct 125.5). sector_depths_by_source verdict is changes_within_a_source, not a calibration offset, so the dip is not steady across sectors.
Individual transit depths are inconsistent even within a sector; chi2 40.90670645685778 on 5 dof means the 6 transits themselves do not lie on a single depth, with top 3 carrying 0.912 of signal.

Strong secondary dip at phase 0.6148 with depth 336.8 ppm and depth_over_dip 0.6045, plus phase_curve amplitude 159.5 ppm (ratio_to_depth 0.2863, chi2 34.57/9) indicates a close binary with ellipsoidal/beaming variability, not a planet.
Odd vs even depths differ (422.7 ppm odd vs 700 ppm even, ratio 1.7, difference 0.3961), supporting a binary at twice the detected period or variable eclipses, not a planet transiting once per orbit.
